name: The Fall of Apartheid: South Africa's Long Struggle
description: From Zulu kings and Boer wars to Sharpeville, Soweto and Mandela's election: how a system of racial law was built, resisted and brought down.

checkpoints.name: Kingdoms and conquest
checkpoints.note: The Zulu Kingdom rose in the early nineteenth century and fought Britain in the Anglo-Zulu War of 1879. After the Second Boer War of 1899 to 1902 Britain held the whole region, and Black South Africans were left with few political rights.

checkpoints.name: Laws of separation
checkpoints.note: The Union of South Africa formed in 1910 as a state run by its white minority. The African National Congress was founded in 1912, and Gandhi, who had lived in South Africa for years, left in 1914. After 1948 the government built apartheid, dividing people by race in law.

checkpoints.name: Banned and imprisoned
checkpoints.note: In 1960 police killed protesters at Sharpeville, and the government banned the African National Congress. Nelson Mandela and other leaders were tried at Rivonia in 1963 and 1964 and sentenced to life in prison.

checkpoints.name: Uprising
checkpoints.note: In 1976 school students in Soweto protested and were met with gunfire. Steve Biko, a leader of the Black Consciousness movement, died in police custody in 1977. Desmond Tutu, an Anglican churchman who later became archbishop of Cape Town, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984 and urged peaceful pressure on the government.

checkpoints.name: A new South Africa
checkpoints.note: Mandela was freed in 1990 and talks began. In 1993 the Nobel Peace Prize went to him and F. W. de Klerk, and in 1994 South Africa held its first election open to all adults, won by the ANC. Cyril Ramaphosa, a negotiator of the new constitution, became president in 2018.
